clue.text: Ambitions Drake nurtured of leaving The Golden Hind?

indicators.note: letters that are nurtured are brought up and reshaped, so these two words are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Sir Francis Drake harboured big dreams once he stepped off his famous ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nurtured' is the anagram signal on AMBITIONS and DRAKE, fourteen letters in all. The Golden Hind was Drake's ship, so stepping off it is a getting-ashore.
explanation.definitionFit: Going ashore from a vessel such as Drake's galleon is the act of landing passengers from a ship.

clue.text: Feeling of distrust about the French close-fitting garment

indicators.note: about means one piece wraps around the other here, the distrust word going round the French article

parts.note: doubt is a feeling of distrust
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A suspicious mood surrounds a snug French item of clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A doublet was a snug jacket worn by men from the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries.

clue.text: Loose T-shirt tops handy for girl in pool?

indicators.note: loose suggests the letters are let free and rearranged, so the three words are shuffled together

explanation.surface: Baggy tees and tops are useful for a girl at the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: The pool is not for swimming: it is a typing pool, the office room of secretaries who took dictation in a quick script.
explanation.definitionFit: Typing pools were staffed by secretaries trained in speed-writing and typewriting, mostly women in the mid-twentieth century.

clue.text: May, in France, meet North Sea

parts.note: mai is the French word for the month of May

explanation.surface: In France, May sees the meeting of the North Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meet' is a link word; 'the main' is an old poetic name for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry and old seafaring language the open ocean is called the main, as in the Spanish Main.

clue.text: Abolishes article missing from year-books

indicators.note: missing from tells us the article is dropped out of the longer word for year-books

parts.note: annuals are books published once a year
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone scraps a piece left out of some yearly publications.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul something is to cancel or declare it void, so abolishes is a synonym.

clue.text: How Japanese store beer as a souvenir

parts.note: to keep something is to store it
sake is the Japanese rice drink, brewed like a beer

explanation.surface: A question about the way Japanese people save their brew, answered with a memento.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How Japanese' sets up the reading: the Japanese would keep their sake. Sake is made by brewing rice, so it is often called rice beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A memento kept to remember a person or occasion is a souvenir.

clue.text: It responds, somehow, this condition 1-having been treated by numbers

definitions.text: this condition 1-having been treated by numbers

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters arrive in some unspecified new order, so the two words are anagrammed

explanation.surface: A patient reacts in some way to a state brought on by numbing drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The '1-' is most likely a printed dash. 'numbers' are things that numb, such as anaesthetics, not figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluggish inactivity and numbness, the state of being dulled, is what a numbing anaesthetic produces.

clue.text: Unique occasion during term?

parts.note: an event that happens only one time within a whole life span, a 'term' read as the term of one's existence

explanation.definitionFit: A one-off event that will never come again is said to happen just one time in all your years.

clue.text: Bumble, perhaps, and be lead astray

indicators.note: led astray means sent off course, so the letters of the two words wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A dithering person might well lead someone off the right path.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bumble is the pompous parish officer in Dickens's Oliver Twist, so 'perhaps' marks him as an example; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Bumble in Oliver Twist holds the post of parish officer who keeps order, a famous example of the role.

clue.text: Moreish sort of state?

parts.note: Moreish read as 'belonging to Thomas More', whose 1516 book describes an ideal island commonwealth

explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas More's book named an imaginary perfect society, and an idealised state is described with the adjective from it.

clue.text: Otalgia from having to wear a cheeked cap

indicators.note: having means holding within, so the run of words contains the letters needed

explanation.surface: An ear complaint caused by wearing a cap with cheek flaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'wEAR A CHEeked'; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Otalgia is the medical term for pain in the ear.

clue.text: Unwilling, like many going to hospital

parts.note: a lot means many
H is the standard abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Many people are reluctant to go into hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Being reluctant or disinclined to do something is a synonym, more often spelt loath.

clue.text: CS file said to be made secret for security purposes

indicators.note: to be made signals the letters are made into something new, so the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Civil Service file is reportedly to be restricted for safety reasons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' looks like a homophone signal but is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Documents restricted to authorised people for reasons of national security are officially labelled this way.

clue.text: eg Wensleydale — Eccles showing pretty contours for photographer

parts.note: Wensleydale is a crumbly Yorkshire cheese, an example
an Eccles cake is a round currant-filled pastry from Lancashire

explanation.surface: Two Northern English foods are lined up as if for a glamour shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Wensleydale is a cheese from Yorkshire and an Eccles cake a flaky currant pastry from a Lancashire town. The answer is also slang for photos of shapely women.
explanation.definitionFit: In photography slang the term covers pictures of attractive women posing to display their figures.

clue.text: Retrograde paintings of doubtful repute and worthless

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the word for paintings is read in reverse

parts.note: art means paintings collectively
shy is an old slang word meaning shady or disreputable

explanation.surface: Backward-looking pictures of dubious standing that are of no value.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of poor quality and no value is rubbishy or cheap.

clue.text: Sovereign in identical grasp? Swindlers try it on

indicators.note: grasp means the word for identical holds the monarch inside it

parts.note: same means identical
a king is a sovereign

explanation.surface: A monarch is held in a firm grip while con men try their luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sovereign' tempts as the old gold coin, but here it is the monarch; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigged game or racket used by con artists to cheat the victim is a swindle of this kind.

clue.text: Holding any opinion about men

indicators.note: about means the word for opinion goes round the men

parts.note: a tenet is a belief or opinion held

explanation.surface: Having some view or other about the male sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding' looks like a verb but is a noun: in law the answer is property held by a tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: In law the word means land or property held by tenure, a holding; today it usually means a block of flats.

clue.text: Edgar upset in bed and harassed

indicators.note: in places the shuffled name inside the bed word
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the name is rearranged

explanation.surface: Edgar, unsettled while lying in bed, was pestered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' makes ADGER from EDGAR, which goes inside BED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be pestered persistently is to be hounded, named from the old sport of baiting a burrowing animal.

clue.text: Ambled about in place of uproar

indicators.note: about here means the letters are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone strolled around in a scene of chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. The answer comes from Bethlem, the London madhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a notorious London asylum came to mean any scene of noisy confusion.

clue.text: Rubbing noses is OK with me, if controlled

indicators.note: if controlled suggests the letters are directed and put in order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A speaker agrees to nose-rubbing, provided it is kept in check.
explanation.walkthrough: Nose-rubbing is known as an Eskimo kiss, so the definition works as an adjective, as in 'an ___ kiss'; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Touching noses as a greeting is popularly called an Arctic-style kiss after the Inuit custom.

clue.text: Fruit from Ohio mountain, chains

parts.note: O is a short form for Ohio, used in older US state abbreviations
ranges are chains of mountains

explanation.surface: Produce shipped from Ohio's peaks and ridges.
explanation.definitionFit: Citrus produce from the orange tree are fruit.

clue.text: Deed held by third party English county rising

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the county abbreviation is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Worcs is the abbreviation for Worcestershire, an English county

explanation.surface: A legal document is held in trust while an English shire climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns WORCS into SCROW. Worcestershire is a county in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A bond or deed kept by an independent party until conditions are met is held in this arrangement.

clue.text: Leaving work to study provides light relief

parts.note: day means daylight, light
release means relief, freedom from something

explanation.surface: Taking time off for college gives some welcome respite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provides' is a link. In Britain, employers grant staff time off, typically one day a week, to attend college.
explanation.definitionFit: A British scheme letting employees attend college during working hours, usually a day a week.

clue.text: She gets a rave review

indicators.note: review read as re-view, look at again in another order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actress earns a glowing write-up from the critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rave review' reads as a glowing critique, but 'review' is the anagram signal on RAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so it stands for any female person.

clue.text: Means of spearing a fish

definitions.meaning: a long infantry spear with a pointed head

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a long-shafted infantry weapon and a toothy freshwater predator.

clue.text: Get Mickey moving?

parts.note: Mickey Mouse is a cartoon, so getting him to move means making drawn frames into a film

explanation.definitionFit: To bring cartoon figures to life on screen, as Disney did with his mouse, is to give them motion.

clue.text: Using playful satire, fencing

definitions.meaning: jesting or mocking in a scornful way, from rail meaning to scoff
a fence or barrier of bars

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is mocking or complaining with banter; the other is a barrier of upright bars around a space.

clue.text: Ways of town-criers or cleansing department employees?

parts.note: streets are the roads or ways of a town
weepers are people who cry

explanation.surface: Town criers on their rounds, or council workers cleaning the roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'town-criers' suggests the bell-ringing announcers, but the hyphen is split: town streets plus people who weep. 'or' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Council workers who brush and clean public roads are employed in this job.
